title: Advancing Mass Spectrometry Analyses of Proteins, Assemblies, and Proteoforms
text:
We aim to develop robust analytical technologies that can provide structural information for biologically important
proteins and molecular machines, such as those involved in neurodegenerative disorders and aging (e.g.,
Alzheimer’s disease). New methodologies to elucidate the sites of protein modifications will be developed, with
the knowledge gained on modification sites to be used to enhance our understanding of the cellular mechanisms
for a range of biological processes, including Alzheimer's disease. This is a particularly pressing goal in view of
the rapid aging of our nation’s population and the rising costs of care for patients with neurodegenerative
diseases.

title: Neural basis of behavioral timescale coordination
text:
Long term plans as well as moment to moment dynamic adjustments are a hallmark of flexible behavior 
and the disruption of this ability is a common symptom in many psychiatric illnesses. The brain's 
ability to coordinate between different temporal demands is a neuronal process that is currently 
not well understood and the proposed studies, using a novel unconstrained and quasi-naturalistic 
approach, will fundamentally advance that understanding.

title: BCM CENTER FOR PRECISION MEDICINE MODELS
text:
The introduction of clinical exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing has transformed
our ability to diagnose patients with suspected genetic disease. However, up to 50-70% of
patients with suspected genetic disease remain undiagnosed likely because their disease-
causing variant(s) has yet to be discovered, or the clinical significance of variants identified in
genomic studies remains unclear. The BCM Center for Precision Medicine Models will support
local, national, and international programs and individual researchers in the development of
precision animal models that end the diagnostic odyssey of patients with undiagnosed, rare, and
Mendelian diseases and serve as resources for pre-clinical studies investigating personalized
medicine approaches to their care.

title: Cancer Informatics Shared Resource
text: Cancer Informatics Shared Resource Summary Modern cancer research critically depends on advanced computing, data analysis, and modeling for the generation of basic and translational experimental data; harmonization, secure storage, and retrieval of clinical data; clinical-molecular data integration; and interpretation, annotation, and integration of results. The Cancer Informatics Shared Resource (CISR) provides Masonic Cancer Center (MCC) members with cutting-edge multi-omics data analytics and translational data science, advanced natural language processing research and application development, data storage infrastructure, and expert consulting and collaboration to support all aspects of their research. CISR is a combination of the previous Bioinformatics and Clinical Informatics Shared Resources. It is led by Dr. Jinhua Wang, a Full Professor in the University of Minnesota Institute for Health Informatics and a computational biologist with research interests in computational modeling of high-throughput cancer multi- omics data. He is supported by Dr. Scott Walmsley, who was recruited to lead proteomics/DNA adductomics informatics, and Dr. Steven Johnson, who heads the Clinical Informatics Shared Service (CISS). Additional staff were recruited or promoted, and a genomics data repository was built to link genomic information with clinical health records. CISR will achieve its mission through 5 specific aims: 1) Support MCC researchers with advanced capabilities in cancer multi-omics informatics and clinical data science and analytics, through a FAIR and artificial intelligence/machine learning–ready data environment; 2) Pursue development of new methods in the areas of single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics imaging, and AI deep learning predictive models for cancer research; 3) Enhance clinical trial recruitment via data-driven understanding of the factors determining accrual success and decision models to enhance accrual; 4) Develop and provide integration infrastructure and methods towards developing cancer patient Digital Twins to support predictive oncology research and patient care; and 5) Provide education and training in multi-omics data analytics, spatialomics data integration, and precision oncology. CISR also has close collaborations with the Clinical Trials Office, Translational Therapy Shared Resource, Biostatistics Shared Resource, and the Cancer Research Translational Initiative within MCC, as well as with the Institute for Health Informatics and the Clinical and Translational Science Institute in the larger University community. In fiscal year 2022, 47 individuals used CISR services, of whom 41 were MCC members.

title: Detection and noninvasive monitoring of early stage RGC gene expression changes in glaucoma
text:
Glaucoma represents a series of diseases for which progressive loss of the optic nerve and retinal ganglion cells
(RGCs) is the common endpoint. Glaucoma treatment is hindered by delayed diagnosis, uncertainty about whom
to treat, and inability to predict treatment response. This proposal uses several innovative technologies to
develop techniques for non-invasive detection of early stage RGC gene expression changes to inform when and
in whom to apply vision saving glaucoma therapies.

title: Research and Education Core
text: RESEARCH EDUCATION CORE PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT Cancer is a leading cause of death among the Puerto Rican population. Furthermore, a 142% increase in cancer incidence is anticipated for the Puerto Rican population. Yet, the field of cancer research, composed of many public health and health science disciplines, continues to lack cancer researchers in Puerto Rico, highlighting the urgent need for pathways and necessary structural support to build and advance the cancer research workforce. Through the Partnership’s Addressing Cancer Health Drivers and Infection-Driven Malignancies (ACTION) program, in collaboration with its Research Education Core (REC), we aim to meet the critical need for training and workforce enhancement in cancer research. Our long-term goal is to intervene at career transition points to expand the pipeline at all levels, from undergraduate and graduate to faculty and academic leadership. The overall objective of the REC is to provide pathway opportunities and critical structural support to attract and encourage the continuous, robust engagement of a qualified cohort of students, early-stage investigators, faculty, and research staff focused on cancer-related basic, clinical, translational, and population science research, with a long-term goal of reducing cancer. The REC is based on a 22-year history of Partnership in educational and training activities at our partnering institutions, The University of Puerto Rico (UPR), The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC), and The University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Center (UPRCCC). Our central hypothesis is that the creation of competitive pathway programs that foster trainees toward a career in cancer research enhances i) the career development of trainees by building research skills, ii) competitiveness for obtaining faculty positions, and iii) capacities that will result in advancing innovations in science and expanding the U.S. biomedical workforce. We propose 3 specific aims. These outcomes will result in an expanded and growing scientific workforce to address health drivers in cancers for this community and inform the broader problems of health drivers in cancers across the U.S. Overall, we anticipate an increase in the retention of investigators in Puerto Rico pursuing cancer research, achieving academic leadership roles, and securing funding for the independent researcher stage.

title: Molecular mechanisms behind microbiota regulation of host amino acid and glucose homeostasis
text:
The microbes living on/in the human body, known as “the human microbiota”, metabolize various
dietary nutrients, impact host metabolism, and are essential for human health. This proposal aims
to investigate the molecular mechanisms behind microbiota-Type 2 diabetes (T2D) association
and provides mechanistic insights of some microbial pathways involved in mediating host amino
acid and glucose homeostasis. It will also pave the way for a systematic regulation of these health-
related microbial pathways in the human gut using synthetic biology and microbial genetics to
treat age-related disease like T2D.

title: DEVELOPMENTAL REGULATION OF FIBROBLAST GROWTH FACTOR-19 IN NEONATES
text:
Preterm infants have immature gastrointestinal function, small bile acid pools, and adrenal insufficiency that
limit their development and response to enteral nutrition. Fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19) is a potent fetal
growth factor that is upregulated postnatally and functions to regulate bile acid homeostasis. In this proposal,
we seek to determine the impact of perinatal glucocorticoids and FGF19 on gastrointestinal, hepatic and
metabolic outcomes in preterm pigs.

title: Enabling Discovery-Based Brain Metabolomics with Ultra-High Resolution Liquid Chromatography and Machine Learning
text:
Cocaine use disorder is one of the most challenging disorders for society to address due to its rapid progression
and lack of approved treatments/therapies. Identifying the neurochemical changes arising from this chronic
disorder will be beneficial for providing early medical intervention for those affected; however, current technology
is not capable of discovering these chemical alterations. In this project, we will develop new instrumentation and
data analysis techniques that enhance our ability to monitor neurochemicals in the living brain and address
questions relating to the underlying cause of cocaine use disorder within an animal model for addiction.

title: Core D: Translational Imaging Core
text:
The Translational Imaging Core (TIC) will offer novel quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 
techniques and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) with a variety of novel radiotracers to SPORE 
investigators for the noninvasive characterization of renal cell carcinoma in animal models and patients and 
for the assessment of the response to therapies. A sophisticated radiogenomics platform to co-register MRI 
and PET/CT images with tumor specimens will allow targeted tissue procurement informed by imaging 
features detected in vivo. The TIC will provide a web-based centralized archive and image analysis 
capabilities for all imaging data acquired in SPORE projects.

title: Clinical Neuroscience Research Training Program in Psychiatry
text:
Mental illness affects approximately 15% of the population, creates enormous disability and cost, and has been
stubbornly persistent over the decades. To fundamentally alter this trajectory we must recruit and train the
next generation of physician-scientist researchers who will generate the advances in diagnosis, treatment,
prevention, and cure that we need to alleviate this burden. Yale’s T32-funded Clinical Neuroscience Research
Training Program, of which this is a renewal application, has an exceptional track record of training psychiatric
physician-scientists, which we here aim to continue and enhance.

title: The role of breast stem cells in early stages of breast carcinogenesis
text:
Throughout a woman’s life, the breast tissue structure is maintained by a population of so-called stem cells
with self-renewal capacity; these cells have also been linked to unfavorable tumor characteristics and poorer
breast cancer outcomes. We propose a highly novel investigation that will comprehensively examine the role of
stem cells lineages in early stages of breast cancer development. Findings from this study could be used to
improve breast cancer risk prediction in a large segment of high-risk women undergoing routine breast
biopsies and those with dense breast tissue which could pave a way for novel personalized breast cancer
prevention and surveillance strategies.

title: Characterizing Newly Identified Human Cytomegalovirus Entry Receptors
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) causes major disease in neonates and transplant patients. Understanding
HCMV entry into host cells is paramount in terms of designing vaccines. Our studies will characterize HCMV
proteins that mediate virus entry, proteins that are likely some of the best targets for anti-HCMV vaccines.

title: Overcoming Treatment Resistance by Targeting Polyploid Breast Cancer Cells with AI assisted Single-Cell Analysis
text:
We aim to reduce breast cancer treatment resistance by targeting polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs), a highly
resilient subpopulation strongly associated with poor clinical outcomes. To achieve this, we will enhance our
single-cell morphological analysis platform by integrating deep learning, enabling robust and scalable detection
of PGCCs across diverse staining protocols and imaging systems. Leveraging this enhanced pipeline, we will
systematically prioritize and rigorously validate candidate anti-PGCC compounds using patient-derived cancer
cells, 3D tumor spheroids, and both syngeneic and xenograft mouse models, driving translational progress
toward more effective breast cancer therapies.

title: Determining the Postfertilization Regulatory Functions of a Sperm microRNA Cluster
text:
Due to their limited cytoplasmic contents, historically sperm were considered to be mere carriers
of the paternal genome; however, research in the past decade has revealed that sperm
microRNAs (miRNAs) are not only important to development, but also are sufficient for the
transfer of paternal non-genetically inherited phenotypes to progeny. The Fx-miRs are a cluster
of miRNAs whose expression in sperm is highly conserved and who influence early
development. By using preimplantation embryos and mouse embryonic stem cells as an in vitro
model of early developmental cells, I will determine the capacity of the Fx-miRs to regulate
targets through translation, as well as the direct targets of these miRNAs and the downstream
effects of those binding events to reveal the first mechanistic functions of these sperm miRNAs.

title: Optimizing Use of Advanced Diabetes Technology for Self-Management in Adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes: Integration of Real-Time Glucose and Narrative Data
text:
Improving glycemic control and psychosocial well-being in adolescents is essential to preventing complications
and mortality associated with type 1 diabetes. In this project, we will develop an ecological momentary
intervention to optimize adolescents’ use of advanced diabetes technology for self-management. The
knowledge generated through this project will contribute to the advancement of self-management behaviors
and improve health outcomes for individuals with type 1 diabetes.

title: Effects of exercise training on subcutaneous adipose tissue cellular heterogeneity in adults with obesity
text:
Limited lipid storage in abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue (ASAT) leads to excessive fatty acid release,
promoting ectopic fat deposition and cardiometabolic complications in obesity. While endurance training may
enhance ASAT lipid storage capacity and improve cardiometabolic health, the underlying cellular and
molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This project will investigate whether a 3-month endurance training
intervention increases the abundance, modifies the transcriptional profile and spatial localization, and
enhances lipid uptake capacity of a distinct adipocyte subtype in adults with obesity.

title: RP1: Host responses to melioidosis and B. pseudomallei virulence determinants
text: Project Summary – RP1 Burkholderia pseudomallei (Bpm), a Gram-negative facultative intracellular pathogen, is responsible for melioidosis, a disease with high morbidity and mortality rates. Although Bpm is most often acquired via inhalation, it can also infect through ingestion or percutaneous inoculation. The pathogen poses significant public health risks due to its increasing incidence, particularly in diabetes and immunosuppressed populations, and its resistance to traditional antibiotics. Despite Bpm’s classification as a biothreat agent and its deadly nature, the mechanisms of its lung infection and dissemination remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap hinders efforts to prevent and treat infections, especially in endemic regions. The long-term objective of this research is to comprehensively analyze host-pathogen interactions during Bpm lung infections and identify virulence factors crucial for pulmonary infection and immune system interactions. The hypothesis is that Bpm- specific virulence factors expressed in the lungs trigger immune responses, influencing the pathogenesis of the disease. The study consists of three specific aims: (1) to evaluate virulence and disease progression of clinically relevant Bpm isolates linked to pulmonary infection using murine models, (2) to characterize host- pathogen interactions in vivo by analyzing Bpm’s protein and transcriptional responses, and (3) to investigate the role of Bpm virulence factors in lung inflammation and macrophage polarization. The research employs advanced techniques such as immunohistochemistry, RNA-seq, and transposon mutant screening to evaluate the bacterial and host responses. Results will reveal novel virulence factors, their impact on host inflammatory responses, and potential biomarkers for diagnostic and therapeutic applications. This work will advance our understanding of Bpm pathogenicity, aiding in the development of targeted therapies and preventive measures against melioidosis.

title: SYNcronized Agentic Prescriptive System for Improving Sequentially HIV Care Continuum (SYNAPSIS-HIV-CC)
text:
SYNAPSIS-HIV-CC addresses a critical gap in HIV care by developing an innovative artificial intelligence system
to overcome the limitations of current predictive models. By integrating agentic and causal AI, large language
models, and knowledge graphs with extensive multimodal data, SYNAPSIS-HIV-CC aims to provide novel and
important clinical tools to help with the HIV clinical care continuum.

title: Integrated Systems Biology of Pediatric AML
text:
Relevance Statement:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is the second most common childhood leukemia and has a dismal prognosis. For over 40
years AML chemotherapy has changed little with the continued reliance on ara-C, daunorubicin and etoposide as
frontline agents. The proposed research seeks to define the impact of proteomic and metabolomics landscape of
leukemic cells on patient risk stratification and revealing additional layers of the molecular basis of AML prognosis
to guide the development of more effective treatments for AML.
